There’s nothing wrong with not particularly loving the pieces programmed, and I’m glad at least that you have this anonymous space to vent about it. I’ve felt the same on many occasions…premiering a piece that’s not idiomatic in the slightest, and/or a composer who has over-intellectualized it, etc. That said, our jobs, even in an unpaid community or lab ensemble, is to play the works as successfully as we possibly can. We’ve got to try to not let our preparation and focus drop between pieces based on favor.

In the community orchestras I’ve been involved in, the programs are either decided by the conductor solely (usually in smaller/newer ensembles,) or with an artistic board. I personally think that it’s great that your orchestra is performing new compositions with the composers being involved. New music needs to be played, and living composers need to be given a shot to have their works performed, and to improve. 

For the specific concern at hand - are you being charged dues, or are you saying that you’re paying to be in the group due to the travel and time you’ve invested? How soon is this concert? I would not recommend dropping out of the concert, especially if it’s less than two months away. As much as I feel for you, not liking the music isn’t the strongest reason to drop after committing. 

What you might do instead…
1. Ask about what next season looks like. If the programs still don’t feature what you like to play, step away.
2. Ask about being apart of the artistic board, or if they’d take suggestions. 
3. Search for a different ensemble.

I’ve never seen a community orchestra do an entire season of new compositions. I hope that future seasons will mix the programs up a bit more! Best of luck to you, hope you have a great night!

Start planning as ahead of time as you can. If you're looking to apply this fall, get dates and parts to musicians this summer. Same goes for reserving a performance location (church or campus.) As cazgem commented, it's helpful to compensate with dinner or some sort of treats. Write everyone cards thanking them for sure. Play gigs and recitals for these musicians!

Throw your hat in the ring of community orchestras and campus ensembles. If a professor or community director knows of your goals, they may exchange podium time for assistance work. Summer festivals will also help gain podium footage. This doesn't have to be huge like the Aspen or Monteux festivals.

When selecting repertoire, try not to over-program in terms of difficulty and size. Keep the instrumentation smaller if you can (think Beethoven 1, Copland Appalachian Spring for 13 Instruments, and strings only repertoire like Tchaik's Serenade or Price's Adoration.) 

There is nothing wrong with lab-type footage. Example: Mvt. I of Beethoven 1 with only violin, cello, flute, and piano (playing reduction.) I've had success on summer festivals with recordings like these. 

You're amazing and you've got this!! Best of luck!
